question: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, over what arc of the horizon must a masthead light show an unbroken white light?
choice_a: 360 degrees, visible from every direction
choice_b: 112.5 degrees, from right ahead to the beam on one side only
choice_c: 45 degrees, directly over the bow only
choice_d: 225 degrees, from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on either side
explanation: Rule 21 defines a masthead light as an unbroken white light over an arc of 225 degrees, fixed to show from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on either side of the vessel.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.21 (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 21 - Definitions)

question: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, over what arc must each sidelight (red port, green starboard) show an unbroken light?
choice_a: 112.5 degrees, from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on its respective side
choice_b: 225 degrees, covering both sides of the bow
choice_c: 360 degrees around the entire horizon
choice_d: 67.5 degrees, centered on dead astern
explanation: Rule 21 defines sidelights as showing an unbroken light over an arc of 112.5 degrees, from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on their respective side of the vessel.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.21 (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 21 - Definitions)

question: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, over what arc must a sternlight show an unbroken white light?
choice_a: 225 degrees, matching the masthead light
choice_b: 135 degrees, centered on dead astern (67.5 degrees on each side)
choice_c: 112.5 degrees, matching a single sidelight
choice_d: 360 degrees, matching an all-round light
explanation: Rule 21 defines a sternlight as a white light placed as nearly as practicable at the stern, showing an unbroken arc of 135 degrees centered on dead astern.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.21 (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 21 - Definitions)

question: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, how is an 'all-round light' defined?
choice_a: A light that flashes at least 120 times per minute
choice_b: A light visible only from directly astern
choice_c: A light showing an unbroken light over an arc of the horizon of 360 degrees
choice_d: Any light used exclusively while at anchor
explanation: Rule 21 defines an all-round light as one showing an unbroken light over the full 360-degree arc of the horizon, such as an anchor light or a combined masthead/stern light on a small vessel.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.21 (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 21 - Definitions)

question: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, how is a 'flashing light' defined?
choice_a: Any light that blinks at an irregular rate
choice_b: A light flashing at exactly 60 flashes per minute
choice_c: A light that stays on continuously but changes color
choice_d: A light flashing at regular intervals at a frequency of 120 flashes or more per minute
explanation: Rule 21 defines a flashing light as one flashing at regular intervals at a rate of 120 or more flashes per minute -- for example, the all-round flashing yellow light an air-cushion vessel must show when operating in the non-displacement mode.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.21 and 83.23(b) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rules 21 and 23)

question: Under Inland Rule 22, from what minimum distance must the masthead light of a power-driven vessel less than 39.4 feet (12 meters) long be visible on a dark, clear night?
choice_a: 2 miles
choice_b: 1 mile
choice_c: 5 miles
choice_d: 6 miles
explanation: Rule 22 requires the masthead light of a vessel less than 12 meters (39.4 feet) in length to be visible from at least 2 miles on a dark, clear night, even though that same small vessel's sidelights need only be visible from 1 mile.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.22 (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 22 - Visibility of Lights)

question: Under Inland Rule 22, from what minimum distance must the masthead light of a vessel 164 feet (50 meters) or more in length be visible on a dark, clear night?
choice_a: 2 miles
choice_b: 6 miles
choice_c: 3 miles
choice_d: 10 miles
explanation: Rule 22 requires the masthead light of a vessel 50 meters (164 feet) or more in length to be visible from at least 6 miles on a dark, clear night, the longest required visibility range for any navigation light.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.22 (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 22 - Visibility of Lights)

question: For a vessel less than 39.4 feet (12 meters) long, how does the required visibility distance of its sternlight compare to that of its sidelights under Inland Rule 22?
choice_a: Both must be visible from exactly the same distance of 1 mile
choice_b: The sidelights must be visible farther than the sternlight
choice_c: The sternlight must be visible 2 miles, while the sidelights need only be visible 1 mile
choice_d: Neither has a minimum visibility distance on vessels under 39.4 feet
explanation: Under Rule 22, a vessel under 12 meters (39.4 feet) must have a sternlight visible from 2 miles, a longer range than the 1-mile minimum required for its sidelights.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.22 (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 22 - Visibility of Lights)

question: Under Inland Rule 23, which power-driven vessels are required to exhibit a second masthead light, positioned higher and abaft the forward one?
choice_a: Only vessels under 23 feet
choice_b: All power-driven vessels regardless of size
choice_c: Only vessels operating exclusively at anchor
choice_d: Vessels 164 feet (50 meters) or more in length; smaller vessels may show one but are not required to
explanation: Rule 23(a) requires a power-driven vessel underway to show a second masthead light abaft of and higher than the forward one, except that a vessel less than 50 meters (164 feet) is not obliged to exhibit it, though it may do so.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.23(a) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 23 - Power-Driven Vessels Underway)

question: A special Inland Rule provision lets power-driven vessels operating on the Great Lakes -- including Lake Michigan, part of Illinois's waters -- substitute what for the second masthead light and sternlight?
choice_a: An all-round white light shown where the second masthead light would be, with equivalent range
choice_b: No light of any kind is required on the Great Lakes
choice_c: A red flashing light at the bow
choice_d: Two green sidelights instead of the usual red-and-green pair
explanation: Rule 23(e) permits a power-driven vessel operating on the Great Lakes to carry an all-round white light in lieu of the second masthead light and sternlight, in the position where the second masthead light is normally located.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.23(e) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 23 - Power-Driven Vessels Underway)

question: Under Inland Rule 23, what additional light must an air-cushion vessel (such as a hovercraft) exhibit while operating in the non-displacement mode?
choice_a: A second red sidelight at the stern
choice_b: An all-round flashing yellow light where it can best be seen
choice_c: No additional light is required in non-displacement mode
choice_d: A steady blue light at the bow
explanation: Rule 23(b) requires an air-cushion vessel operating in the non-displacement mode to exhibit, in addition to the lights required for power-driven vessels, an all-round flashing yellow light where it can best be seen.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.23(b) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 23 - Power-Driven Vessels Underway)

question: Under Inland Rule 25, what optional additional lights may a sailing vessel underway exhibit at or near the top of the mast, and what restriction applies to using them?
choice_a: A single flashing amber light, which may be combined with any other option
choice_b: Three white lights in a triangle, required on every sailing vessel
choice_c: Two all-round lights in a vertical line, red over green, but not in combination with the single tricolor masthead lantern
choice_d: A green light only, replacing the sidelights entirely
explanation: Rule 25(b) allows a sailing vessel underway to exhibit two all-round lights in a vertical line at or near the top of the mast, red over green, but this option may not be used together with the combined tricolor masthead lantern permitted under the same rule.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.25(b) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 25 - Sailing Vessels Underway and Vessels Under Oars)

question: Under Inland Rule 25, what day shape must a sailing vessel display forward when it is also being propelled by machinery (motor-sailing)?
choice_a: A ball shape at the stern
choice_b: Two balls in a vertical line
choice_c: No day shape is ever required on a motor-sailing vessel
choice_d: A conical shape, apex downward
explanation: Rule 25(e) requires a vessel proceeding under sail while also being propelled by machinery to exhibit forward, where it can best be seen, a conical shape, apex downward; vessels under 12 meters (39.4 feet) are not obliged to show it but may do so.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.25(e) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 25 - Sailing Vessels Underway and Vessels Under Oars)

question: Under Inland Rule 30, which anchored vessels are NOT eligible to use the single all-round white light option, and must instead show the full two-light configuration (forward light or ball, plus a lower light at or near the stern)?
choice_a: Vessels 164 feet (50 meters) or more in length
choice_b: Vessels less than 23 feet in length
choice_c: All sailboats, regardless of length
choice_d: Personal watercraft only
explanation: Rule 30(b) allows a vessel less than 50 meters (164 feet) in length to show a single all-round white light instead of the two-light forward/stern configuration in Rule 30(a); vessels 50 meters or more must use the full two-light configuration.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.30(a)-(b) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 30 - Anchored Vessels and Vessels Aground)

question: Under Inland Rule 30, what additional obligation applies to an anchored vessel 328 feet (100 meters) or more in length?
choice_a: It is exempt from showing any anchor light at all
choice_b: It shall also use available working or equivalent lights to illuminate its decks
choice_c: It must sound a whistle continuously while anchored
choice_d: It must display red and green sidelights while at anchor
explanation: Rule 30(c) provides that a vessel at anchor may, and a vessel 100 meters (328 feet) or more in length shall, use available working or equivalent lights to illuminate its decks.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.30(c) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 30 - Anchored Vessels and Vessels Aground)

question: Under Inland Rule 30, when is a vessel less than 23 feet (7 meters) long completely exempt from exhibiting any anchor light or shape?
choice_a: It is never exempt, regardless of location
choice_b: Only between sunrise and sunset
choice_c: When anchored somewhere other than in or near a narrow channel, fairway, anchorage, or where other vessels normally navigate
choice_d: Only if the vessel is unpowered
explanation: Rule 30(e) exempts a vessel less than 7 meters (23 feet) in length, when at anchor and not in or near a narrow channel, fairway, anchorage, or where other vessels normally navigate, from exhibiting any anchor lights or shapes.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.30(e) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 30 - Anchored Vessels and Vessels Aground)

question: Under Inland Rule 30, what additional lights (and shapes, if practicable) must a vessel aground display, beyond its normal anchor light?
choice_a: A single flashing green light at the bow
choice_b: No additional lights are ever required for a grounded vessel
choice_c: A continuously sounding siren instead of any light
choice_d: Two all-round red lights in a vertical line, and three balls in a vertical line
explanation: Rule 30(d) requires a vessel aground to show its normal anchor lights plus, if practicable, two all-round red lights in a vertical line and three balls in a vertical line; vessels under 12 meters (39.4 feet) are exempt from this additional signal.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.30(d), (f) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 30 - Anchored Vessels and Vessels Aground)

question: Under Inland Rule 30, vessels under what length are exempt from showing anchor lights and shapes when anchored in a special anchorage area designated by the Coast Guard?
choice_a: Less than 65.6 feet (20 meters)
choice_b: Less than 23 feet (7 meters)
choice_c: Less than 328 feet (100 meters)
choice_d: No length-based exemption exists for special anchorage areas
explanation: Rule 30(g) exempts a vessel less than 20 meters (65.6 feet) in length from exhibiting anchor lights and shapes when anchored in a special anchorage area designated by the Coast Guard.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.30(g) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 30 - Anchored Vessels and Vessels Aground)

question: Under Inland Rule 33, at what minimum vessel length is a whistle required to be carried on board?
choice_a: 65.6 feet (20 meters) or more
choice_b: 39.4 feet (12 meters) or more
choice_c: 328 feet (100 meters) or more
choice_d: A whistle is required on every vessel regardless of length
explanation: Rule 33(a) requires a vessel 12 meters (39.4 feet) or more in length to carry a whistle meeting the specifications of Annex III to the Inland Rules.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.33(a) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 33 - Equipment for Sound Signals)

question: Under Inland Rule 33, at what minimum vessel length must a bell be carried in addition to a whistle?
choice_a: 39.4 feet (12 meters) or more
choice_b: 23 feet (7 meters) or more
choice_c: 65.6 feet (20 meters) or more
choice_d: A bell is never required under the Inland Rules
explanation: Rule 33(a) requires a vessel 20 meters (65.6 feet) or more in length to carry both a whistle and a bell.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.33(a) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 33 - Equipment for Sound Signals)

question: Under Inland Rule 33, at what minimum vessel length must a gong be carried in addition to a whistle and bell?
choice_a: 65.6 feet (20 meters) or more
choice_b: 39.4 feet (12 meters) or more
choice_c: A gong is required on every vessel with a bell
choice_d: 328 feet (100 meters) or more
explanation: Rule 33(a) requires a vessel 100 meters (328 feet) or more in length to carry a whistle, a bell, and a gong whose tone cannot be confused with that of the bell.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.33(a) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 33 - Equipment for Sound Signals)

question: Under Inland Rule 33, what is required of a vessel less than 39.4 feet (12 meters) long that is not equipped with a whistle or bell?
choice_a: It must have some other means of making an efficient sound signal
choice_b: It is exempt from making any sound signal under any circumstance
choice_c: It must instead display a flashing red light
choice_d: It must return to shore immediately
explanation: Rule 33(b) exempts a vessel less than 12 meters (39.4 feet) in length from carrying the sound-signaling equipment prescribed in Rule 33(a), but requires it to have some other means of making an efficient sound signal.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.33(b) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 33 - Equipment for Sound Signals)

question: Under Inland Rule 32's definitions, approximately how long is a 'short blast' of a vessel's whistle?
choice_a: About 4 to 6 seconds
choice_b: About 1 second
choice_c: About 10 seconds
choice_d: About 30 seconds
explanation: Rule 32(b) defines a short blast as a blast of about 1 second's duration, distinguishing it from a prolonged blast.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.32(b) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 32 - Definitions)

question: Under Inland Rule 32's definitions, how long is a 'prolonged blast' of a vessel's whistle?
choice_a: A blast of about 1 second's duration
choice_b: A blast of exactly 2 seconds' duration
choice_c: A blast of from 4 to 6 seconds' duration
choice_d: Any blast longer than 30 seconds
explanation: Rule 32(c) defines a prolonged blast as a blast of from 4 to 6 seconds' duration, used for signals such as the bend signal and the restricted-visibility signal for a vessel making way.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.32(c) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 32 - Definitions)

question: Under Inland Rule 34, when power-driven vessels in sight of one another are meeting or crossing, what does one short blast of the whistle mean?
choice_a: I intend to leave you on my starboard side
choice_b: I am operating astern propulsion
choice_c: I am altering course to starboard
choice_d: I intend to leave you on my port side
explanation: Rule 34(a) provides that one short blast means 'I intend to leave you on my port side' when power-driven vessels in sight of one another are meeting or crossing within half a mile of each other.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.34(a) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 34 - Maneuvering and Warning Signals)

question: Under Inland Rule 34, when power-driven vessels in sight of one another are meeting or crossing, what does two short blasts of the whistle mean?
choice_a: I intend to leave you on my starboard side
choice_b: I intend to leave you on my port side
choice_c: I am operating astern propulsion
choice_d: Danger -- I do not understand your intentions
explanation: Rule 34(a) provides that two short blasts mean 'I intend to leave you on my starboard side' when power-driven vessels in sight of one another are meeting or crossing.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.34(a) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 34 - Maneuvering and Warning Signals)

question: Under Inland Rule 34, what does three short blasts of the whistle mean?
choice_a: I intend to leave you on my port side
choice_b: I am operating astern propulsion
choice_c: I am nearing a blind bend
choice_d: I am leaving a dock or berth
explanation: Rule 34(a) provides that three short blasts mean 'I am operating astern propulsion,' warning nearby vessels that the vessel is backing.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.34(a) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 34 - Maneuvering and Warning Signals)

question: Under Inland Rule 34's overtaking signals, what does one short blast from the overtaking vessel indicate?
choice_a: It intends to overtake the other vessel on that vessel's port side
choice_b: It is unable to overtake and is stopping
choice_c: It intends to overtake the other vessel on that vessel's starboard side
choice_d: It is sounding the danger signal
explanation: Rule 34(c) provides that, in an overtaking situation, one short blast from the overtaking vessel signals its intent to overtake on the other vessel's starboard side, while two short blasts signal intent to overtake on the port side.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.34(c) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 34 - Maneuvering and Warning Signals)

question: Under Inland Rule 34, what sound signal must a vessel give if it fails to understand another vessel's intentions or doubts whether sufficient action is being taken to avoid collision?
choice_a: One prolonged blast only
choice_b: Three short blasts
choice_c: No signal -- silence is required to avoid confusion
choice_d: At least five short and rapid blasts
explanation: Rule 34(d) requires a vessel that doubts another vessel's intentions, or believes insufficient action is being taken to avoid collision, to immediately sound at least five short and rapid blasts -- the danger or doubt signal.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.34(d) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 34 - Maneuvering and Warning Signals)

question: Under Inland Rule 34, what signal must a vessel sound when nearing a bend in a channel or fairway where other vessels may be hidden by an obstruction, and how must it be answered?
choice_a: One prolonged blast, answered with a prolonged blast by any approaching vessel within hearing
choice_b: Five short blasts, answered with silence
choice_c: Two short blasts, answered with three short blasts
choice_d: No signal is required at blind bends under the Inland Rules
explanation: Rule 34(e) requires a vessel nearing a bend where other vessels may be obscured by an intervening obstruction to sound one prolonged blast, which must be answered with a prolonged blast by any approaching vessel within hearing around the bend.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.34(e) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 34 - Maneuvering and Warning Signals)

question: Under Inland Rule 34, what signal must a power-driven vessel sound when leaving a dock or berth?
choice_a: Two prolonged blasts
choice_b: One prolonged blast
choice_c: Three short blasts
choice_d: No signal is required when leaving a dock
explanation: Rule 34(g) requires a power-driven vessel leaving a dock or berth to sound one prolonged blast.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.34(g) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 34 - Maneuvering and Warning Signals)

question: Under Inland Rule 35, what sound signal must a power-driven vessel making way through the water sound in restricted visibility, and how often?
choice_a: Two prolonged blasts, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes
choice_b: One prolonged blast followed by two short blasts, at intervals of not more than 1 minute
choice_c: One prolonged blast, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes
choice_d: Continuous ringing of a bell
explanation: Rule 35(a) requires a power-driven vessel making way through the water in restricted visibility to sound one prolonged blast at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.35(a) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 35 - Sound Signals in Restricted Visibility)

question: Under Inland Rule 35, what sound signal must a power-driven vessel that is underway but stopped, making no way through the water, sound in restricted visibility?
choice_a: One prolonged blast every 2 minutes, the same as a vessel making way
choice_b: Five short and rapid blasts
choice_c: One short blast every minute
choice_d: Two prolonged blasts in succession, with about a 2-second interval between them, repeated at intervals of not more than 2 minutes
explanation: Rule 35(b) requires a power-driven vessel underway but stopped and making no way through the water to sound two prolonged blasts in succession, about 2 seconds apart, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes -- distinguishing it from a vessel still making way.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.35(b) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 35 - Sound Signals in Restricted Visibility)

question: Under Inland Rule 35, which vessels sound one prolonged blast followed by two short blasts (instead of the normal power-driven vessel signals) in restricted visibility?
choice_a: A vessel not under command, restricted in her ability to maneuver, a sailing vessel, a vessel fishing, or a vessel towing or pushing another vessel
choice_b: Only vessels at anchor
choice_c: Only vessels aground
choice_d: Only pilot vessels on pilotage duty
explanation: Rule 35(c) requires a vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, a sailing vessel, a vessel engaged in fishing, or a vessel towing or pushing another vessel to sound, instead of the signals in Rule 35(a) or (b), one prolonged blast followed by two short blasts at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.35(c) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 35 - Sound Signals in Restricted Visibility)

question: Under Inland Rule 35, what sound signal must a manned vessel being towed (the last vessel of the tow, if more than one is towed) sound in restricted visibility?
choice_a: The same single prolonged blast used by a vessel making way
choice_b: Four blasts in succession: one prolonged followed by three short blasts
choice_c: No signal -- only the towing vessel is required to signal
choice_d: Continuous rapid bell ringing
explanation: Rule 35(e) requires a manned vessel being towed -- or the last vessel of the tow, if more than one is towed -- to sound four blasts in succession, one prolonged followed by three short, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.35(e) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 35 - Sound Signals in Restricted Visibility)

question: Under Inland Rule 35, what sound signal must a vessel at anchor give in restricted visibility, and how often?
choice_a: One prolonged blast every 2 minutes, the same as a vessel underway
choice_b: Five short and rapid whistle blasts every minute
choice_c: Ring the bell rapidly for about 5 seconds, at intervals of not more than 1 minute
choice_d: No sound signal is required while at anchor
explanation: Rule 35(g) requires a vessel at anchor to ring the bell rapidly for about 5 seconds at intervals of not more than 1 minute; a vessel 100 meters (328 feet) or more in length must also sound a gong in the after part of the vessel immediately afterward.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.35(g) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 35 - Sound Signals in Restricted Visibility)

question: Under Inland Rule 35, what must a vessel aground sound in restricted visibility, beyond the bell signal required of an anchored vessel?
choice_a: Nothing extra -- the anchor bell signal alone is sufficient
choice_b: Five short and rapid whistle blasts instead of the bell
choice_c: One prolonged blast every 2 minutes
choice_d: Three separate and distinct strokes on the bell immediately before and after the rapid ringing
explanation: Rule 35(h) requires a vessel aground to give the anchor bell (and gong, if required) signal, plus three separate and distinct strokes on the bell immediately before and after the rapid ringing; it may also sound an appropriate whistle signal.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.35(h) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 35 - Sound Signals in Restricted Visibility)

question: Under Inland Rule 35, a vessel less than 39.4 feet (12 meters) long that does not carry the bell prescribed for anchor/aground signals must instead do what in restricted visibility?
choice_a: Make some other efficient sound signal at intervals of not more than 2 minutes
choice_b: It is completely exempt from making any sound signal
choice_c: It must display a flashing light instead of any sound signal
choice_d: It must leave the water immediately
explanation: Rule 35(j) provides that a vessel less than 12 meters (39.4 feet) in length is not obliged to give the bell signals of Rule 35(g)-(h), but if it does not, it must make some other efficient sound signal at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.35(j) (Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 35 - Sound Signals in Restricted Visibility)
